# Results — Study 286 (Valentines-Day) on the ^GSPC daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Valentine's trading
sessions are hardcoded in [`data.py`](../valentines_day/data.py) (1950–2025, 76
years). ^GSPC daily close-to-close returns (price-only) are from the repo-level
cache `_cache/^GSPC_split_only.parquet`. Match the fingerprints below to confirm
you hold the same data. As-of **2026-06-17**.*

## Data stamp

| Source | Window | n observations | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| ^GSPC daily close-to-close (price-only) — Valentine sessions | 1950–2025 | 76 events | `23a6d0b41333` |
| ^GSPC daily close-to-close (price-only) — full window (baseline) | 1950–2025 | ~19,100 days | `ca0a9a85212a` |
| Valentine session-date table | 1950–2025 | 76 rows | hardcoded constant |

## The unconditional daily mean — the key number

The honest baseline is **not** zero. The S&P 500 drifts up a hair every session:
the unconditional daily mean over 1950–2025 is **+0.0364%/day** (≈3.6 bps), with a
~0.99%/day standard deviation. Any "is Valentine's Day positive?" claim that tests
against zero gets the market's whole-day drift for free. The correct question is
whether the Valentine session beats **+0.0364%**, not whether it beats 0.

## Valentine's session vs the baseline (primary spec)

| Arm | n | mean return | up-rate |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Valentine session (roll-forward from Feb 14) | 76 | **+0.0388%** | **47.4% up** |
| Unconditional daily | ~19,100 | +0.0364% | 53.1% up |

- **Excess mean: +0.24 bps/day** — the Valentine session beats the average day by
  about a quarter of a basis point. That is noise: it is **0.7%** of one day's
  standard deviation.
- **Up-rate is actually *lower*** on Valentine's Day (47.4%) than on an average day
  (53.1%). The "market loves Valentine's Day" folklore has the sign of the hit-rate
  backwards.
- **One-sample t vs 0: t = +0.352** (p = 0.726) — the raw Valentine return is not
  even distinguishable from zero.
- **One-sample t vs the unconditional mean: t = +0.022** (p = 0.983) — the excess
  return is indistinguishable from the market's ordinary drift.
- **Newey-West (HAC, lag 4) t on the excess return: t = +0.021** — far below the
  desk's |t| ≥ 2 REAL hurdle.
- **Permutation p (10,000 random 76-session draws, two-sided): p = 0.981** — the
  Valentine mean lands dead-centre in the null distribution.

## Sub-periods

| Window | n | Valentine mean | up-rate |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 1950–1987 | 38 | +0.0125% | 36.8% |
| 1988–2025 | 38 | +0.0652% | 57.9% |

The two halves disagree wildly (one below the baseline, one above), which is exactly
what 38-observation noise looks like. There is no stable Valentine premium to point at.

## Turnover & tradability

The only implementable rule is "buy the Valentine's session once a year" (enter at
the prior close, exit at the Valentine close — a one-session hold). Turnover is one
round-trip per year.

- **Gross mean per event: +3.88 bps.**
- **One-way cost 1 bp × NAV (round-trip 2 bps): net mean +1.88 bps/event.** Costs
  eat roughly half of an already-vanishing gross "edge". Borrow is moot (long-only).
- Against the obvious benchmark — that same one day of buy-and-hold — there is
  nothing to harvest: the gross event return *is* the buy-and-hold day. The rule
  only adds cost.

## Positive control

On a synthetic daily tape (Mon–Fri calendar) with a **planted Valentine premium**,
the same engine fires cleanly: at +10 bps/day the excess is recovered with HAC
t ≈ 2.9 and permutation p ≈ 0.009; at +25 bps, HAC t ≈ 6.2, p < 0.001. At
premium = 0 the engine correctly finds nothing (HAC t ≈ 0.7, p ≈ 0.5). The null
result on the real tape is a statement about the **market**, not the method.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** Excess mean +0.24 bps/day, HAC t = +0.02, perm p = 0.98,
  t vs unconditional = +0.02. The Valentine session is statistically identical to an
  average day — and its up-rate (47%) is actually *below* the 53% base rate.
  *Signal-axis caveat:* price-only index, vendor back-revises the ^GSPC level; this
  can only flatter, not rescue, a non-result.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** No vehicle beyond "be long the S&P for one pre-chosen
  February day"; the ~4 bps gross edge is noise and one-way costs halve it. Passive
  buy-and-hold of that same day is strictly better.
- **Busted — folklore.** The market does not love Valentine's Day. There is a faint
  positive drift, but it is the market's everyday drift, present on every session.
